claims.text: Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering temperatures above 2300 °C.
Residual porosity in conventionally prepared ZrB2 leads to hole formation during prolonged liquid plating-bath exposure.
Hole formation during prolonged plating-bath exposure eventually causes component failure.
Adding approximately 1–2 wt% Si to ZrB2 will enable densification at 2100–2200 °C.
Adding approximately 1–2 wt% Si will reduce the residual porosity of ZrB2.
Si forms a transient Si-rich liquid or eutectic during sintering of ZrB2.
The transient Si-rich liquid enhances particle rearrangement and consolidation during sintering.
Liquid-assisted particle rearrangement produces better densification at lower sintering temperatures.
Residual Si segregates at ZrB2 grain boundaries and forms passivating films.
Si-rich grain-boundary films reduce pore connectivity and seal microstructural defects.
Reduced pore connectivity blocks infiltration by the liquid plating bath.
Si-doped ZrB2 sintered at 2100–2200 °C will have similar or better densification than conventional ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C.
Si-doped ZrB2 will form fewer holes during long-term liquid plating-bath exposure than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
Si-doped ZrB2 will retain better structural and mechanical integrity during long-term plating-bath exposure than conventionally prepared ZrB2.
The reduced-temperature preparation should be performed in vacuum or an inert atmosphere.
The intervention can lower the sintering temperature without introducing deleterious secondary phases or compromising single-phase ZrB2.
A controlled comparison will use undoped ZrB2 sintered above 2300 °C and 1–2 wt% Si-doped ZrB2 sintered at 2100–2200 °C.

The hypothesis is rejected if Si-doped ZrB2 fails to show a statistically significant reduction in porosity and hole formation or fails to improve mechanical integrity relative to the conventional control.

contradictions.description: The mechanism requires residual Si-rich grain-boundary films, which constitute a compositionally distinct residual phase, while the boundary requires preservation of single-phase ZrB2 without deleterious secondary phases.
